holidays.name: Pasta Day (World Pasta Day)
holidays.description: A global carb-fueled celebration of spaghetti, penne, fusilli and every noodle shape in between. Pasta lovers around the world twirl their forks in unison.
holidays.origin: World Pasta Day was launched at the first World Pasta Congress in Rome in 1995, organized by the International Pasta Organisation to promote pasta as a healthy, affordable staple. It is now observed on October 25 by that group, but many calendars and food fans also celebrate pasta on October 17 in the U.S.
holidays.funFact: Italy has more than 300 different pasta shapes, and Italians eat roughly 23 kilograms (about 50 pounds) of pasta per person each year.

holidays.name: International Day for the Eradication of Poverty
holidays.description: A UN-recognized day when people gather for events, art, and conversations about ending poverty. Not wacky, but it is the day's most globally significant observance.
holidays.origin: Commemorates the 1987 gathering of over 100,000 people at the Trocadéro in Paris, where a plaque was unveiled honoring victims of extreme poverty. The UN officially designated the day in 1992.
holidays.funFact: The commemorative stone from the 1987 Paris gathering has been replicated in cities around the world, and people gather at copies of it each year.

holidays.name: Wear Something Gaudy Day
holidays.description: A day to dig out your loudest, flashiest, most over-the-top outfit and wear it proudly. Sequins, clashing patterns, and neon accessories are all encouraged.
holidays.origin: An unofficial, lighthearted observance that circulates in quirky holiday calendars, encouraging people to ditch tasteful fashion for a day of glorious excess.
holidays.funFact: The word 'gaudy' may come from the Latin 'gaudium' meaning joy, so wearing gaudy clothes is technically joyful dressing.

holidays.name: Mulligan Day
holidays.description: A day for second chances: redo a mistake, retake a bad decision, or try again at something you botched. Golf-style do-overs are fair game.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance inspired by the golf term 'mulligan', a free extra shot after a bad one. It is listed in many quirky holiday calendars as a day to forgive yourself and start fresh.
holidays.funFact: The origin of the term 'mulligan' is disputed, with one popular story crediting a Canadian golfer named David Mulligan in the 1920s who got a do-over from his friends.

holidays.name: Black Poetry Day
holidays.description: A celebration of Black poets and their contribution to literature, honoring voices from Phillis Wheatley to modern spoken-word artists.
holidays.origin: Observed on October 17 to mark the birthday of Jupiter Hammon, born in 1711 and considered the first published Black writer in America.
holidays.funFact: Jupiter Hammon published his first poem, 'An Evening Thought,' in 1761, nearly 15 years before Phillis Wheatley's first book was released.
